transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, hello, doctor. It's nice to meet you too. I, um, well, I came in today because... well, it's about my church. I go every Sunday, have for years and years, and we always have a nice potluck downstairs in the fellowship hall after the service. I'm always one of the ladies helping out, setting things up, because I like to be useful, you know? I've always been a worker. 

But lately, I just... I don't know what's getting into me, but I keep doing these odd things while I'm there. Just really strange things. Like the other Sunday, I was standing right there by the potluck table, supposed to be serving the casserole, and I just stopped. I held the big serving spoon straight up in the air and I wasn't moving. Just standing there completely still with the spoon held up. 

And then another time, I was at the end of the table and I was just folding the same stack of napkins over and over again. Just folding and smoothing and folding the exact same paper napkins, and there was a whole line of people just standing there waiting on me to finish so they could get their plates and sit down, and I just kept folding. It's just so embarrassing, doctor, having everybody looking at me while I'm acting so peculiar, and I just don't understand why I can't just serve the food normally like I always used to do. It just makes me feel so foolish when they have to wait on me like that.
When this happens, are you aware of what is going on around you?

Well, see, that's the thing that really bothers me, doctor. I... I think I am aware, but it's like I'm trapped in a fog or something. I can hear the murmur of the congregation, you know, Mrs. Higgins asking if the green bean casserole is ready, and Pastor Thomas clearing his throat the way he does when he's getting impatient. I can hear the clinking of the silverware and the squeak of those folding chairs we've had since 1998. I know they're all right there, and I know I should just put the spoon down or hand over the napkins. 

But it's like... like my body just won't listen to what my brain is telling it to do. I'm standing there, holding that spoon up, and inside my head I'm screaming, 'Martha, put the spoon in the dish! Serve the food!' but my arm just stays locked right up there in the air. And with the napkins, I can see the line of people, I can see little Timmy Jenkins practically bouncing on his toes waiting for a plate, but my hands just keep smoothing those creases. I'm there, I know I'm there, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, doctor, just being stuck inside yourself while everyone watches.
Before one of these episodes starts, do you ever get a strange feeling, like an unusual smell, taste, or rising sensation in your stomach?

Well, no, doctor, I don't think I do. I mean, I've thought about it, naturally, because you just want some sort of warning, don't you? Some little sign that tells you, 'Martha, it's about to happen again.' But there's just... nothing. No strange smells, thank goodness. My sister Agnes, rest her soul, she used to get these terrible migraines, and she'd always smell burnt toast right before one came on. I always thought that was the strangest thing, smelling something that isn't there, but she swore by it. She'd say, 'Martha, check the toaster,' and I'd know she needed to go lie down in a dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes. 

But for me, with this... this freezing up business, there's no burnt toast. No funny tastes in my mouth either. I still have my morning coffee, just a half cup with a splash of milk, and maybe a piece of dry toast or half a grapefruit if they're on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, and it all tastes perfectly normal. And my stomach... well, my stomach gets a little fluttery sometimes, but that's just nerves, isn't it? Like when I have to read the announcements in front of the whole congregation because Mary Ellen is out sick with her sciatica again. But it's not a rising feeling or anything peculiar like that before I get stuck holding the spoon. 

It just... it just happens. One minute I'm scooping the casserole—and it's a heavy casserole, doctor, made with three cans of cream of mushroom soup and those crispy fried onions on top, just the way the pastor likes it—and the next minute, I'm just frozen. No warning, no funny feelings, just... stuck. I wish there was a warning, I really do. Maybe then I could at least put the spoon down first so I wouldn't look quite so ridiculous standing there like a statue. But no, nothing like that at all.
After one of these episodes ends, can you remember what happened during it?

Well, yes and no, doctor. It's... it's a very strange thing to try and explain. I remember being there, like I said, I remember the sounds and the people waiting, but when it's over, it's almost like waking up from a daydream that you didn't know you were having. Like... like when you're watching television, maybe one of those nice Hallmark movies, and you just sort of drift off for a second, and then you blink and you're back, but you know you missed a piece of the story. 

I remember being frozen, holding that spoon up, and I remember little Timmy Jenkins bouncing around, but then... it's like a jump in time. Suddenly my arm is down, or I'm putting the napkins in the basket, and I have to sort of catch my breath and figure out how much time has passed. Did I stand there for ten seconds? A minute? Five minutes? I just don't know. 

Mrs. Higgins, she's a dear, she usually just pats my arm and says, 'Take your time, Martha, dear,' and that's usually what snaps me all the way back. But the actual time I spent frozen... it's just a blank space. A little hole in my memory right there in the middle of the fellowship hall. And it's so unsettling, doctor, to lose time like that, even if it's just a few moments. It makes me wonder what else I might be forgetting, you know? Like, did I leave the stove on at home? Did I lock the front door? If my brain can just switch off while I'm holding a serving spoon full of mushroom casserole, what else is it doing without my permission? It's just... it's just very worrying, that's what it is.
When you freeze like that, if someone tries to move your arm, does it stay where they place it?

Well, see, that's just the thing, doctor, and it's what really finally made me make this appointment and come in to see you. Because at church, I just keep doing these odd things, and it's getting so embarrassing. Like I said about standing by the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up and just... not moving. Or the napkins! Folding the same stack of napkins over and over again while people are just standing there, waiting on me. 

And to answer your question about moving my arm... well, yes. That's exactly what happened last Sunday, actually. I was frozen there with the spoon, holding it right up over the casserole dish, and Mary Ellen—she was feeling a bit better, her sciatica must have eased up because she was back at church—she came up beside me. She didn't make a fuss, bless her heart, she just gently took my elbow and sort of guided my arm down closer to the dish. And... it just stayed there. Exactly where she put it. 

It was the strangest feeling. I didn't resist her, my arm didn't feel stiff or heavy, it just... moved where she pushed it and then stopped again. Like I was a mannequin in one of those department store windows downtown, you know? The ones at Macy's where they dress them up for Christmas. She moved my arm, and I just stayed in that new position, still holding the spoon, still not scooping the casserole, just hovering an inch above the crispy onions instead of up in the air. I stayed like that until Mrs. Higgins finally patted my shoulder and I sort of snapped out of it. But yes, if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me, like a doll. It's just not right, doctor, a grown woman acting like a statue while the whole congregation is waiting for their lunch.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Voices? Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't heard anything like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, of course. I had to ask Reverend Thomas to speak up just last week during the sermon because he gets to leaning on the pulpit and his voice just drops down to a mumble, and I couldn't hear a word he was saying about the Good Samaritan. But as for hearing people who aren't there... no. 

I live alone, you see, since my husband Henry passed—it'll be twelve years this November, God rest his soul—so the house is very quiet. Sometimes too quiet, if I'm being honest. That's why I like to keep the television on, or the radio in the kitchen when I'm doing my baking. Just for a little background noise, you know? But it's always Bob Barker on The Price is Right or the local news anchors, never... never strange voices just speaking to me out of thin air. 

I did have a neighbor once, Mrs. Gable, who lived two houses down, and she swore she could hear her late mother telling her how to prune the rose bushes, but I always just thought she was a bit eccentric. Or maybe just lonely, bless her heart. But no, for me, there's nothing like that. Just the usual creaks and groans of an old house settling, and the refrigerator humming, and sometimes the neighbor's dog barking at the mailman. But no voices, thank goodness. I think I'd be absolutely terrified if I started hearing someone talking in my living room when I knew the doors were all locked tight. That would just be the icing on the cake with all this freezing up nonsense, wouldn't it? But no, my mind might be playing tricks on my body, making me stand still like a statue, but it hasn't started making up voices yet.
Have you been feeling very depressed lately?

Well, depressed? No, doctor, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I have my moments, of course, just like anybody else who's getting up there in years and living all on their own. When my Henry first passed away, oh, I was in a terrible state for a long while. I'd just sit in the parlor and let the days go by without even opening the curtains, just watching the dust settle on his favorite armchair. But that was grief, you know, and the Good Lord and time do their work with that. 

Lately? No, I don't feel hopeless or sad in that heavy sort of way. I still get up every morning at six o'clock sharp, I make my pot of Folgers, I put on my face, and I make sure the bird feeders out back are full. The bluejays have been just ravenous this week, and if I were truly depressed, I don't suppose I'd care a lick about whether they got their black oil sunflower seeds, would I? I still love my garden, and I still love baking my casseroles. 

Now, I will say I've been feeling awfully frustrated. And embarrassed, too, like I was saying about the church potlucks. It's a heavy thing to carry, worrying about when my body is just going to decide to turn into a mannequin again, and it does make me a bit nervous to go out. Sometimes I think to myself, Martha, maybe you should just stay home today so you don't end up frozen over the ambrosia salad and making a scene. But I force myself to go because I love seeing Mary Ellen and Mrs. Higgins and the rest of the ladies. 

My sister Margaret, now she had real depression back in the nineties. She wouldn't wash her hair, wouldn't answer the telephone for days on end, she just pulled the covers right up over her head and shut the whole world out. It was a terrible worry for all of us, bringing her casseroles she wouldn't even touch. But I'm not doing anything like that. I want to be out and about, doctor, I really do. I have too much living left to do to be hiding under the bedsheets. I just want to figure out why I keep pausing like a broken television set so I can get back to enjoying my life properly without all the church ladies whispering about me. So no, I'm not depressed. Just... very bothered and worn out by all this freezing business, that's all.
Has anyone ever told you that during one of these episodes, you seemed unresponsive when they spoke to you?

Well, yes, actually. That goes right back to what I was telling you when I first sat down, doctor, and it's the whole reason I finally made this appointment in the first place. Because, like I said, I just keep doing these odd things at church, like standing by that potluck table holding the serving spoon up in the air and just... not moving at all. Or folding that exact same stack of napkins over and over again while folks are just standing there waiting on me to move along. 

Well, during that napkin business—they were the nice yellow ones we bought for the spring luncheon, with the little white lilies printed on the corners, very pretty but very thin paper—Mrs. Higgins told me later that she had been standing right across from me. She said she asked me, "Martha dear, could you hand me the salt shaker?" And apparently, I didn't say a peep. She said she asked me three separate times, doctor! Three times! And she told me I just kept right on creasing that same paper napkin, looking right through her like she wasn't even there. 

Mary Ellen said the exact same thing about the casserole incident with the spoon. Before she finally took my elbow and pushed my arm down, she said she had been saying my name. "Martha? Martha?" Just like that, in a loud whisper so as not to cause a scene. And I didn't answer her. I didn't even blink, according to her. 

It’s just so mortifying. I was raised to always answer when spoken to, it’s just common courtesy, you know? My mother would have tanned my hide if I ever ignored a grown woman looking right at me, let alone an elder in the congregation. But to hear them tell it, I was completely unresponsive, just off in my own world, doing those odd little repetitive things or standing like a statue while the whole buffet line is held up. It makes me sound so incredibly rude, but I promise you I don't mean to be! I just... I don't even realize they're talking to me until I finally snap out of it and see them all staring.
After one of these spells, do you feel confused for a while?

Confused? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel confused at all. It's not like... well, you know how sometimes you fall asleep in your recliner in the middle of the afternoon, maybe with the television running, and you wake up and the room is all dim and for just a split second you don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Friday night? It is absolutely nothing like that. 

When I snap out of one of these little spells, I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. Like with the serving spoon at the potluck. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. 

My brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. 

I remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. If I was truly confused, I wouldn't have known to apologize, would I? I wouldn't have known she was waiting on me to move along the buffet line. So no, no confusion in my head, doctor. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.
Have you ever been told you have a brain or nerve problem, such as seizures or epilepsy?

Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, "Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit," but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. 

I actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. 

And as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. 

So whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.
During these spells, have you ever been told that you smack your lips or make chewing movements?

Smack my lips? Oh, my goodness, no. No, doctor, nobody has ever mentioned anything like that to me. If I was standing up there at the potluck table smacking my lips like a cow with the cud, well, Mary Ellen would have certainly told me. She doesn't miss a single trick, that woman, and she's not shy about pointing out a person's flaws, let me tell you. 

But no, when Mrs. Higgins was talking about the napkin incident, she just said I was staring blankly right through her. She didn't say a single word about my mouth moving. I actually make a point never to chew on anything unless I am properly seated at a dining table. My mother always said that chewing gum or smacking your mouth in public was just the absolute height of bad manners, especially in the house of the Lord! Can you imagine? 

I mean, I do have a partial lower plate—I got it about five years ago when my back teeth finally gave out on me, probably from too many of my Aunt Betty's peanut brittle squares at Christmastime over the years, she always made them entirely too hard—and I know sometimes folks with dentures might move their mouths around or smack their lips if the fit isn't quite right. You see it all the time with the older folks over at the care center. But my plate fits just beautifully. Dr. Evans made sure of it, took three separate molds just to get it perfect. 

So no, my mouth is just shut tight when these little spells happen. Just the freezing up and the staring, no chewing on thin air. If I was making odd faces or smacking my lips at Mrs. Higgins on top of ignoring her, I think I just would have died of embarrassment right then and there! It's bad enough just standing there like a bump on a log holding a serving spoon, don't you think?
Have you been diagnosed with any brain illness, such as a stroke, head injury, brain tumor, or encephalitis?

Oh, a stroke or a tumor? Goodness gracious, no. No, doctor, nothing like that has ever happened to me. I've never had a stroke, and I've certainly never had a brain tumor or... what was the other one? Encephalitis? I don't even rightly know what that is, to tell you the truth, but I know I've never had it. 

My brain has always been perfectly fine, just like I was telling you before. Dr. Miller always said I was healthy as a horse, right up until he moved to Florida. And even my new doctor, Dr. Patel—she’s a very sweet young woman, very thorough, always asks about my diet and tells me I need to eat more leafy greens, which I do try, I really do, I put spinach in my salads now instead of just iceberg lettuce—she’s never found a single thing wrong with my head. 

I did bump my head once, though, now that I think about it. It was back in... oh, it must have been 1982, because it was the year of that terrible blizzard. I was out shoveling the front walk, just trying to clear a little path for the mailman, and I slipped on a patch of black ice right near the bottom step. Down I went, and I gave the back of my head a good whack on the concrete. I saw stars for a minute, I really did, and I had a lump the size of a goose egg for a week. My husband, bless his heart, he was so worried he made me lay on the couch with a bag of frozen peas on my head all afternoon. But I never went to the hospital for it, never passed out, and I certainly didn't have any lasting damage. It was just a silly slip on the ice. 

But as far as real illnesses go? Tumors or strokes? No, absolutely not. My friend Brenda, she had a mild stroke a few years back, and it was just awful. The whole left side of her face drooped, and she couldn't talk right for months. She had to do all that speech therapy and physical therapy, learning how to hold a fork again. It was a terrible ordeal for her family. But I don't have anything like that. I can talk just fine, obviously, and my face is perfectly even. It's just these spells where I freeze up like a statue, like I told you. Other than that, my brain is as healthy as can be.
Have these freezing spells started only after another medical problem began, such as an infection, a fever, or another illness?

An infection? Or a fever? Oh, goodness me, no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. Like I was just saying, I have always had the constitution of a workhorse. I haven't even had so much as the sniffles in I don't know how long! 

Well... I suppose my youngest grandson, little Petey, he did have a terrible chest cold right around Thanksgiving. Just hacking and coughing all over the dinner table, bless his heart, he's only five and hasn't quite mastered covering his mouth yet. My daughter Susan was just beside herself, she kept trying to force me to take this awful elderberry syrup she buys at that expensive health food store. Tastes exactly like old shoes, if you ask me! But I told her, I said, "Susan, I do not need that snake oil," and wouldn't you know it, I didn't catch a single thing from him. Not a cough, not a sneeze, and certainly no fever. I haven't run a fever since... oh, it must be twenty years now. 

So no, these strange little pausing spells didn't come on after any sort of sickness or infection. They just started happening all on their own, right out of the clear blue sky. I was perfectly healthy, going about my business, making my potato salad, and then suddenly I'm just getting stuck like a statue for no rhyme or reason. There wasn't any bug or virus that brought it on, I can promise you that. I always make sure to get my flu shot down at the Walgreens every single October anyway, right when they put the little cardboard signs out on the sidewalk. The pharmacist there, Kevin, he has such a gentle hand, you barely even feel the needle go in, and he always asks after my hydrangeas. But no, no fevers or infections here, doctor. Just the freezing up.
During one of these freezing spells, are you able to speak if someone asks you a question?

Speak? Oh, heavens no. That's exactly why I finally decided I needed to come in and see you, doctor, because of these odd things I keep doing at church and how I can't even answer folks when they talk to me. 

Like I was saying before about the potluck table... when I get stuck just standing there, holding the serving spoon up in the air and not moving an inch, folks will come right up to me. Mary Ellen or somebody might ask, "Are you going to serve that?" or "Is there any of the macaroni salad left?" and I just... I don't say a single solitary word back to them. It's like my voice is just as frozen as my arm! 

And it was the exact same way with the napkins. I know I mentioned Mrs. Higgins earlier, but what happened was I just stood there folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. Just creasing them, unfolding them, and folding them right back up, like I was in some sort of trance. And there was a whole line of people waiting on me to move so they could get to the silverware! They were standing right there waiting, saying, "Excuse me," and asking if I was feeling alright, and I just kept right on folding those napkins without making a peep. 

I can't tell you how rude it makes me feel, looking back on it. My mother, rest her soul, she would have tanned my hide if I ever just flat-out ignored someone who was speaking directly to me. It's the absolute height of bad manners! But during those little spells, I just can't seem to get a word out. I'm just stuck doing these odd things while everyone waits on me, and I can't even say "I'm sorry" or "Just a minute, please." It’s entirely out of my hands, I just can't speak at all until the spell passes.
Did these freezing spells begin soon after a major emotional stress or upsetting event in your life?

Well... now that you ask it like that, yes. Yes, there was something just awful that happened. It breaks my heart to even talk about it, to be perfectly honest with you, doctor. 

You see, my dearest friend in the whole wide world... well, we sang in the church choir together. We were both altos, and we stood right next to each other on the second riser every single Sunday for, oh, it had to be near on thirty years. She was the only one in the whole congregation who could hit the low notes in our hymns without sounding like a bullfrog, bless her soul. We did just about everything together. We would carpool to practice on Thursday nights, and she would always bring those little hard butterscotch candies in her purse, the ones wrapped in the yellow cellophane, to keep our throats from getting dry during the long sermons. 

But she passed away. It was just a terrible, terrible shock to all of us. And that was... let me think, it was right before the spring jubilee, so it's been about 11 months ago now. Eleven long months without her. It was just the most upsetting thing I've ever been through in all my days, losing her like that. When she died, it felt like a piece of me just went right with her. I cried for days and days, I couldn't hardly eat my supper, and the church just felt so empty without her standing there next to me. 

And you know, you're exactly right. I hadn't really put two and two together until you just asked, but that is exactly when this whole change started. These spells, the freezing up like a statue and getting stuck at the potluck table... it’s been going on since my closest choir friend died, about 11 months ago. I was just so overcome with the grief of it all, and then suddenly I started having these pauses where I couldn't move or speak. It all started right after I lost her. I just haven't been the same since she passed.
When someone touches you or calls your name during one of these spells, does that ever make the spell stop right away?

Touch me or call my name? Well, no... no, that doesn't seem to break the spell at all, doctor. Like I was telling you just a minute ago about how I keep doing these odd things at church... it's just so embarrassing. I'll be right there by the potluck table, just standing there holding the serving spoon up in the air, not moving a single muscle. And folks will come right up to me, they'll say, "Martha, Martha, are you alright?" They'll say my name clear as day, and Mary Ellen even put her hand right on my shoulder last Sunday when I was stuck like that. She gave me a little shake, a gentle one, of course, because she's a sweet woman, but it didn't do a lick of good. I just stayed frozen there with the spoon.

And it's the exact same thing with those napkins. I told you about how I was folding that same stack of napkins over and over again, just creasing and unfolding and folding them back up while people were waiting. Well, Mrs. Higgins, she got so impatient—you know how she gets when she's hungry—she actually reached out and tapped my arm. She tapped me right on the elbow and said, "Martha, dear, we need to get to the silverware." But even with her tapping me and calling my name, I just kept right on folding. It didn't snap me out of it one bit. I just have to wait until the spell decides to pass on its own, no matter what anybody does to try and wake me up from it. It's like I'm locked inside myself until it's good and ready to let me go.
Before these freezing spells began, did you ever have a seizure?

A seizure? Oh, heavens, no. No, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what a seizure looks like, you see, because my cousin Earls youngest boy used to get them when he was just a little thing. He would fall right down on the floor and shake all over, and his mother would have to rush over and put a rolled-up towel under his head so he would not bang it on the kitchen linoleum. It was just a terrifying thing to watch, let me tell you, just a terrible fright for everyone in the room. But me? No, I have never had a single thing like that happen to me in all my seventy-one years. 

Before these freezing spells started up... the ones where I just get stuck holding the serving spoon or folding those napkins... well, I was always healthy as a horse, for the most part. I mean, my knees are not quite what they used to be, and I take a little pill in the mornings, but as far as my nerves and my brain went, I was perfectly fine. I never had any kind of fit or seizure or anything where I would shake or fall down. It is just these new spells where I freeze up like a statue that are the problem. I never had any trouble like that before my dear friend passed away. Never a seizure, no doctor, not once in my whole life.
During one of these spells, have you ever found yourself automatically copying someone else’s words or movements?

Copying someone else? Oh, my word, no. No, I don't believe I've ever done anything quite like that. When I get stuck... well, like I was telling you about the potluck table, I'm just frozen in my own little world. I'm not paying a bit of attention to what Mary Ellen or Mrs. Higgins or anybody else is doing. 

I mean, if Mary Ellen was waving her hands around or saying a prayer, I certainly wouldn't start waving my hands or saying the prayer right along with her. I wouldn't even know she was doing it, to be perfectly honest. I'm just locked up tight as a drum, holding my spoon or folding my napkins. I've never caught myself repeating what folks say to me, either. When they ask if I'm alright, I don't say, "Are you alright?" right back at them like some sort of parrot. I just don't say anything at all. 

It's really just the freezing up, doctor. I'm not copying a soul. I'm just stuck exactly how I was when the spell decided to come over me. It's the strangest thing, it really is, but it's just me being frozen, not me trying to mimic anybody else in the room. I can promise you that much.
Have you had any episodes of confusion or memory problems outside of these freezing spells?

Confusion or memory problems? Oh, no, doctor, no... nothing like that at all. My mind is just as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I mean, well, I might forget where I put my reading glasses now and then, but that's just normal for a woman my age, isn't it? I'll set them down by the telephone when Mary Ellen calls, and then I'll spend ten minutes looking for them on the coffee table. But that's not what you mean, I know. 

As far as being confused or losing my memory... no, I remember everything clear as a bell. I remember exactly what happened at the church potluck, who was there, what Mrs. Higgins was wearing—she had on that awful floral print dress she bought at the rummage sale three years ago, the one with the big yellow sunflowers on it. I remember every single detail. I know what day it is, I know who the president is, I know exactly what I need to buy at the grocery store without even making a list. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. 

And as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. So whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.
